chats.answer:
For a beginner who wants to TIG weld both steel and aluminum, I'd recommend a budget AC/DC TIG welder in the 200-amp class.

The important distinction is:

DC TIG: Welds steel, stainless steel, and some other metals, but isn't the practical choice for aluminum.

AC/DC TIG: Welds steel, stainless steel, and aluminum.

High-frequency start: Makes learning easier than scratch-start or lift-start TIG.

Foot pedal: Very useful for controlling heat, especially when welding aluminum.

I'd aim for $500–$900 for the machine if you want something inexpensive but still worth keeping as your skills improve.

chats.answer:
For a beginner who wants to TIG weld both steel and aluminum, I'd recommend a budget AC/DC TIG welder in the $500–$900 range.

The important part is AC/DC:

DC TIG works for mild steel and stainless steel.

AC TIG is what you want for aluminum.

High-frequency (HF) start makes learning TIG much easier than scratch-start.

Pulse and adjustable AC balance are useful, but less important than having a reliable arc and good pedal control.

Avoid the tempting $150–$300 DC-only TIG machines if aluminum is one of your goals.

Don't forget the actual startup cost

Even with a cheap welder, you'll need argon shielding gas, a cylinder, a suitable regulator, tungsten electrodes, filler rods, gloves, and an appropriate welding helmet. Budget roughly $200–$400 extra, potentially more if you buy a new gas cylinder.

Also, 120V power is fine for practicing on thinner metal, but 240V is preferable for thicker aluminum.
